kloppy: load and standardize

notes: The opening entries are linked. Full sources are in the reading list. Real sample: Brisbane vs Perth, 21 December 2024, match 1925299.

title: Loading tracking data
body: Load match metadata and JSONL with kloppy
Retain frame IDs, periods and native metres
Convert to a dataframe for analysis
notes: The figure contains actual dataframe values; velocity columns are derived after loading.

title: Tracking quality and visibility
body: Separate detected from extrapolated positions
Keep missingness and coverage visible
Avoid derivatives across gaps or periods
notes: Red rings mark extrapolated players according to raw is_detected. Coordinates can exist without a direct camera observation. All subsequent models inherit this uncertainty.

title: Plotting a tracking frame
body: Draw the pitch in the data’s coordinate system
Color by team and identify the ball
Check direction before calculating goal-related features
notes: Use actual pitch dimensions. A visually plausible frame is a useful first check, but does not prove identity or position accuracy.

title: Animating a sequence
body: Keep player identities consistent across frames
Use playback to inspect motion and tactical context
Overlay model outputs on the same sequence
notes: Three snapshots are from the real selected clip. The notebook contains a full embedded animation.

title: Possession detection
body: Find the nearest player inside a candidate zone
Use ball motion to distinguish touches from flyovers
Leave ambiguous frames unassigned
notes: Figure is an actual 2 m proximity heuristic, not the full Vidal-Codina or PathCRF method. Pros: transparent and quick. Cons: aerial balls, duels and tracking uncertainty. Compare with supplied possession labels; evaluate timing-aware accuracy.

title: Pass-event detection
body: Detect release, ball travel and reception cues
Track a change between plausible player possessions
Validate event timing against video or labels
notes: The real ball path is annotated at supplied possession endpoints. This is an explanatory candidate sequence, not a validated recovered pass. Pros: converts continuous signals to actionable events. Cons: missing ball data and multi-touch ambiguity.

title: Formation detection
body: Remove team translation with centered coordinates
Separate in-possession and defensive samples
Estimate stable role locations over a window
notes: Real median outfield positions are shown separately by possession. Pros: summarizes organization beyond a team sheet. Cons: averaging mixes roles and game states; these are not asserted formation labels.

title: Player-role and line detection
body: Group longitudinal positions into candidate lines
Assign roles consistently through player exchanges
Treat cluster count as a modeling choice
notes: Ward clustering of real centered x positions into three groups is a teaching baseline. It is not a validated named-formation classifier. Pros: interpretable. Cons: fixed line counts, overlaps and rotations.

title: Phase-of-play segmentation
body: Represent phases as intervals rather than single events
Join intervals to tracking by period and frame
Compare structure and effort within tactical context
notes: The plot shows supplied SkillCorner labels, not predictions from a classifier trained here. Pros: makes context explicit. Cons: taxonomy-dependent and sensitive to boundary definitions.

title: Estimating player speed
body: Smooth positions within valid continuous segments
Differentiate coordinates using elapsed time
Convert m/s to km/h for running bands
notes: Actual speed curves are shown. Pros: foundation for physical and tactical features. Cons: derivatives amplify noise; smoothing removes some short peaks.

title: Distance covered
body: Integrate speed across valid intervals
Distance ≈ Σ speed × Δt
Report coverage alongside the total
notes: The real sample’s cumulative distance excludes missing derivatives. No full-match extrapolation. Pros: simple workload volume measure. Cons: incomplete and extrapolated tracking affect accuracy.

title: High-speed and sprint distance
body: HSR: documented men’s band 20–25 km/h
Sprint: above 25 km/h
Accumulate distance separately in each band
notes: Our code uses [20,25) and [25,infinity) to avoid overlap; exact equality handling is a teaching convention. Pros: distinguishes intensity from volume. Cons: thresholds and exposure affect comparisons.

title: Sprint-effort counts
body: Group consecutive threshold-exceeding frames
Require a stated minimum duration
Define whether brief gaps are merged
notes: Shaded segments are our >=1 s, no-merging teaching rule. They are not exact SkillCorner production sprint counts. Pros: repeated-effort view. Cons: sensitive to thresholds, smoothing and merging rules.

title: Acceleration and deceleration
body: Differentiate scalar speed for speeding up or slowing down
Keep signed acceleration distinct from vector magnitude
Check duration as well as peak acceleration
notes: The plot uses real signed speed derivatives. A direction change can produce acceleration-vector magnitude without increasing scalar speed. Pros: captures bursts and braking. Cons: highly noise-sensitive; threshold crossing alone does not qualify a production explosive effort.

title: Time to high-speed running
body: SkillCorner measures the 9 → 20 km/h interval
Use a qualifying explosive acceleration
Compare the speed trajectory, not just peak speed
notes: The real crossing is illustrative, not production-qualified. The published metric is the minimum interval within qualifying explosive accelerations. Start detection, >0.7 s high-acceleration qualification and filtering matter.

title: Time to sprint
body: SkillCorner measures the 9 → 25 km/h interval
A quick top speed does not imply a quick acceleration
Check the qualifying effort before reporting the metric
notes: Real observed crossing shown. No official Time to Sprint or Top 3 value is reconstructed. Pros: explosiveness/capacity. Cons: limited opportunities, sample size and qualification rules.

title: PSV-99: activity-based speed capacity
body: Use SkillCorner’s defined activity population
Summarize high-speed activity rather than all frames
Do not substitute an all-frame percentile
notes: The real frame-speed distribution illustrates why populations matter. SkillCorner describes PSV-99 over physical activities above 15 km/h. This histogram is not the official PSV-99 calculation.

title: Peak Velocity: absolute top speed
body: Identify the highest reliably measured speed
Inspect the quality of the peak interval
Keep sample maxima separate from production metrics
notes: The figure uses our smoothed sample-speed estimates. It does not reproduce SkillCorner’s validated production Peak Velocity. Pros: interpretable capacity measure. Cons: noisy spikes, short exposure and preprocessing dependence.

title: Expected goals: shot quality
body: Distance and angle form a simple feature baseline
Tracking adds keeper and defender context
Fit and calibrate on many labeled shots
notes: Hypothetical shot rays at a real ball location; no xG prediction is invented. Pros: familiar target and interpretable features. Cons: sparse shots, outcome imbalance and contextual bias.

title: Expected Threat: location value
body: Divide the pitch into states
Combine shooting reward with future movement value
Iterate the transition equation to value continuation
notes: Actual fitted DataBallPy open-play grid, not trained on this small sample. V(s)=P(shot|s)P(goal|shot,s)+sum P(successful move to s'|s)V(s'). Classic location xT does not use defender positions. State the model target and training domain.

title: Expected Threat gained
body: Look up the value at both endpoints
Completed-action value: V(end) − V(start)
Use tracking context to explain what location-only xT misses
notes: The arrow is real ball displacement in the selected clip, not an assertion of a single completed pass. Attack direction is normalized and 105 m scaled to the model’s 106 m convention. Pros: simple action valuation. Cons: path-independent, no defender context or causal attribution.

title: Voronoi space control
body: Assign every location to its closest player
Aggregate player regions by team
Use as a geometric baseline
notes: Actual frame, grid approximation to a Voronoi partition. Pros: quick and interpretable. Cons: hard boundaries and no movement, ball-flight or uncertainty.

title: Gaussian player influence
body: Project influence in the player’s movement direction
Let covariance describe directional reach
Inspect the individual surface before aggregating
notes: Real player velocity with an illustrative ellipse. The covariance is not the exact Fernández/Bornn parameterization. Pros: smooth and motion-aware. Cons: hand-set influence scale and simplified movement ability.

title: Gaussian team control
body: Aggregate individual influence by team
Compare team influence continuously across the pitch
Interpret the result as an influence score
notes: Our logistic transformation bounds the team difference; it is not a calibrated possession probability. Pros: contested-space view. Cons: aggregation and covariance assumptions affect the surface.

title: Arrival-time control
body: Estimate reaction and travel time to each location
Compare the earliest arrival for each team
Test sensitivity to movement assumptions
notes: Actual frame with a simple 0.7 s projection and 5 m/s travel speed baseline. Pros: interpretable timing. Cons: no ball flight, acceleration optimization or interception-rate integration; not Spearman’s full model.

title: Ball-aware pitch control
body: Simulate how long the ball takes to reach a target
Estimate player interception and control over that interval
Combine competing control rates
notes: Architecture schematic on actual tracking context, not a computed Spearman surface. Pros: physical link to passing. Cons: uncertain reactions, speed and ball parameters. Separate from the arrival-time teaching baseline.

title: Expected pass completion
body: Specify a passer and candidate destination
Simulate ball travel and interception opportunities
Evaluate reliability on labeled attempts
notes: Actual accessible-space xC inference on hypothetical endpoints at real teammate positions. Pros: interpretable risk. Cons: model calibration, ball speed and offside conventions; candidates are not observed choices.

title: Accessible space
body: Simulate passes across directions and speeds
Estimate where the attacking team can receive
Integrate accessibility across the pitch
notes: Actual public-model output. Pros: incorporates ball and player movement. Cons: simulation assumptions and resolution; individual access can overlap.

title: Dangerous accessible space
body: Weight accessible locations by goal danger
Integrate to obtain danger-weighted space
Keep danger-weighted area distinct from scoring probability
notes: Actual public-model dangerous surface. Pros: links access and useful territory. Cons: danger definition and physical assumptions; DAS units are danger-weighted square metres.

title: Changes in dangerous space
body: Compare the model on successive real frames
Report AS and DAS on their own scales
Inspect the movements that change available options
notes: Actual model values on three frames. Pros: connects movement to changing opportunity. Cons: different team possession states and model noise must be checked; before/after changes alone are not causal credit.

title: Off-ball run threat
body: Evaluate a run even when no pass is made
SkillCorner’s target considers a run being served
Separate run threat from location-based event xT
notes: Actual supplied xthreat values for off-ball runs. The provider model is not reconstructed. Pros: visible unserved contributions. Cons: counterfactual assumptions, context and selection bias.

title: Tracking as a spatial graph
body: Represent players as nodes
Choose relationships that define spatial edges
Preserve identities while avoiding arbitrary row-order effects
notes: Real radius graph. Pros: models relationships directly. Cons: radius edges miss distant tactical relationships; fully connected and learned connectivity are alternatives.

title: Node and edge features
body: Nodes: position, velocity, team and possession
Edges: distance, relative position and team relation
Normalize and mask missing features explicitly
notes: Actual edge-feature rows. Edge direction controls the sign of relative position. Team IDs should be encoded meaningfully rather than treated as numeric magnitudes.

title: Graph neural message passing
body: Create messages from players and their relationships
Aggregate neighbour messages with shared functions
Update player representations for a prediction task
notes: Architecture schematic, not a trained result. Pros: relational inductive bias and shared updates. Cons: oversmoothing, connectivity choices and training requirements. Attention alone is not causal importance.

title: Temporal node features
body: Add lagged speed, displacement and relative movement
Use rolling history only up to prediction time
Include elapsed time and missing-history masks
notes: Actual one-second lag and speed change on a real player. Explicit lag frame checks prevent bridging gaps. Instantaneous velocity adds motion information but is not a substitute for full history.

title: Dynamic graphs over time
body: Recompute spatial edges as players move
Maintain player identities across snapshots
Model changing passing lanes and defensive relationships
notes: Actual snapshots and a player trail. A sequence of spatial graphs retains team interactions that change with time; a static aggregate passing network does not.

title: Temporal edges between snapshots
body: Link each player to their previous observed state
Retain spatial edges within each frame
Direct historical connections toward the prediction time
notes: Schematic topology with real player IDs. The notebook creates actual spatial and temporal edge records. Do not connect across substitutions or tracking gaps without an explicit rule; labels cannot leak future frames.

title: Recurrent temporal graph models
body: Encode each frame with a spatial GNN
Update a recurrent hidden state as frames arrive
Predict from the accumulated historical state
notes: Architecture schematic rather than a claim about a specific cited model’s GRU implementation. Pros: sequential processing with a compact state. Cons: long-history retention and sequence alignment. No trained inference is shown.

title: Temporal convolution on graph history
body: Stack frame-level graph embeddings over time
Apply causal filters across historical windows
Control the receptive field with layers and dilation
notes: Architecture schematic. Pros: parallel computation and explicit receptive field. Cons: window length, dilation and sampling-rate choices. Filters must not access future frames at prediction time.

title: Causal temporal attention
body: Add time information to historical graph embeddings
Attend to relevant earlier states
Mask future frames and missing observations
notes: Architecture schematic. Pros: flexible history selection and long-range dependencies. Cons: data/computation requirements, masking and leakage; attention weights do not establish causal importance.

title: Spatiotemporal message passing
body: Connect spatial neighbors within each frame
Connect player identities across observed time
Learn updates over both relationship types
notes: General architecture schematic, not a reproduction of PathCRF. Pros: joint relational/time structure. Cons: graph size, identity errors and edge construction choices.

title: SoccerMap: spatial neural prediction
body: Convert tracking into spatial feature channels
Learn field-wide surfaces with convolutional networks
Use distinct heads or models for distinct targets
notes: Architecture schematic. SoccerMap is a convolutional approach, not a GNN. Pros: field-wide outputs. Cons: rasterization and training data requirements; no pretrained inference is claimed.

title: Expected possession value
body: Specify what outcome and horizon value means
Combine action selection, success and continuation
Include the value of failure and turnovers
notes: Conceptual decomposition: sum over actions P(action|state) times outcome-conditional value, including failure. EPV is a framework/target, not a synonym for GNN. Different EPV definitions must not be mixed.

title: Observed passes and supplied EPV
body: Inspect value changes on actual pass events
Compare valuable actions with their tracking context
Keep supplied predictions separate from our calculations
notes: Actual pass_epv_delta_for fields in SkillCorner dynamic events. This is the provider’s model output; not a reconstructed Fernández or DEFCON prediction. The field name is shown rather than assuming undocumented equivalence.

title: DEFCON: defensive contribution
body: Use graph-based models for action components
Estimate the opponent’s possession value
Account for defenders’ contribution to reducing danger
notes: Architecture schematic only. Explain attribution assumptions before interpreting defensive credits. Actual frame is context, not DEFCON inference.

title: U.S. Soccer: counterattack graphs
body: Build graphs from synchronized SkillCorner and events
Define counterattack success explicitly
Evaluate predictions on held-out sequences
notes: Architecture schematic. The published balanced event-frame study uses reaching the penalty area as success; the repository’s additional all-frame dataset has different goal labels. Do not mix those datasets or quote them as equivalent.

title: TacticAI: corner-kick modeling
body: Predict receiver and shot outcomes
Represent player interactions with graph networks
Suggest alternative positional configurations
notes: Architecture schematic. The input illustration uses real tracking near a supplied corner-reception event; it is not the original TacticAI input or trained inference. Complete task-specific code/weights and licensed data are not released. Model-generated suggestions are not guarantees.

title: Trajectory forecasting
body: Encode observed player and team history
Generate multiple plausible continuations
Evaluate geometry, tactical coherence and uncertainty
notes: Architecture schematic; no invented future trajectories are shown as learned output. GenTac is a recent preprint example. Distinguish forecasting and causal intervention.

title: Validating tracking models
body: Split data by matches or independent sequences
Evaluate calibration and task-specific outcomes
Stress-test missingness, direction and parameters
notes: Schematic split only, not measured performance. Event detection needs timing tolerances; probability models need calibration; tactical labels need a clear taxonomy.
